title: Participial constructions and word order

objectives.can: Unpack a chain of participles and separated words in an Augustinian or classical period, and notice what the order emphasises.

explanation.summary: A Latin period often hangs its clauses on participles instead of on conjunctions, and it separates words that belong together. You read such a sentence by finding what each participle agrees with and what the main verb is. The same order that hides the grammar also shows the writer's stress, and this lesson works three sentences from Augustine and one from Cyprian.

sections.heading: A participle is a small clause
body: Latin often puts a small circumstance into a participle that agrees with a noun, where English would use a separate clause. A participle can say when ("after he had …"), why ("since …"), how ("while …", "by …") or in spite of what ("although …"). Nothing in the word itself says which; the sense of the sentence decides, and the English should be chosen to match.

A participle in the nominative agrees with the subject of its sentence: *illi autem affigentes cor caelo manserunt in casa*, 'but those, fixing their heart on heaven, stayed in the hut'. The ablative absolute is the same idea with a noun that has no other part in the sentence: *interiecto … digito … codicem clausi*, 'a finger having been put between the pages, I shut the book'.

Do not confuse a participle with a gerund. *legendo* in *posteaquam legendo et inhiando hausit firmitatem* is an ablative of the gerund, 'by reading and by gazing eagerly'. It is a verbal noun and has no noun to agree with.

sections.heading: Chains of participles: find the noun each agrees with
body: In a long period, several participles may hang from one subject or object. Go through them one at a time. For each participle, find its case, number and gender, then look for the noun in the same form. That noun is what the participle describes.

In Confessions 8.15 two participles stand in parallel halves of one sentence: *trahentes cor in terra abierunt in palatium, illi autem affigentes cor caelo manserunt in casa*. Both are nominative plural. The first goes with Ponticianus and his party, who went back to the palace; the second goes with the two converts, who stayed in the hut; and each describes how its group acted. The finite verbs *abierunt* and *manserunt* are the main verbs; the participles add the manner.

sections.heading: Hyperbaton: words that belong together are separated
body: Latin often puts other words between an adjective or participle and its noun, or between a noun and the genitive that depends on it. The grammar tells you what belongs to what: only a form with the same case, number and gender can be joined.

In *quasi luce securitatis infusa cordi meo omnes dubitationis tenebrae diffugerunt*, the ablative noun *luce* and its participle *infusa* are held apart by the genitive *securitatis*; the dative *cordi meo* then follows; and the subject *omnes … tenebrae* is split by the genitive *dubitationis*. The sense is: as though a light of security had been poured into my heart, all the shadows of doubt fled. The separation holds the reader in suspense and puts the climactic verb at the very end.

sections.heading: Order and emphasis: first place, last place, verb last
body: The most important positions in a Latin clause are the first and the last. The verb often comes last, and then the whole picture is built up before the action falls. Putting a word first, before the verb, marks it as the point of the sentence. In Cyprian, *ad regnum caelorum non potest peruenire discordia* puts the goal first and the subject, *discordia*, last: the subject is the thing to be stressed, and it is withheld until the end.

A subject can also be delayed by an interruption. In Confessions 8.27 *aperiebatur … casta dignitas continentiae* is interrupted by two relative clauses, and then the subject is followed by a string of nominative adjectives and participles (*serena*, *hilaris*, *blandiens*, *extendens*) that all describe it.

sections.heading: Antithesis and parallel clauses
body: Augustine and Cyprian often set two thoughts side by side in clauses built alike, so that the opposed words are in matching places. *sed illud placebat et uincebat, hoc libebat et uinciebat* gives two pairs of verbs of the same shape, and the sound of *uincebat* ('it won') and *uinciebat* ('it bound') plays on the difference of one letter. In *ligatus non ferro alieno, sed mea ferrea uoluntate*, 'bound not by another's iron but by my own iron will', the repeated *ferro … ferrea* makes the contrast of outer and inner bondage.

Chiasmus is the crossed order A B … B A. It is a figure to watch for, but do not look for it everywhere. Many of the matching pairs in these authors are simply parallel (A B … A B), and the name of the figure matters less than what the position shows you.

sections.heading: A routine for a period
body: 1. Find the finite verbs. 2. Choose the main verb. 3. List every participle, gerund and gerundive, and give each its case, number and gender. 4. Find the noun it agrees with and ask whether it stands for a time, a cause, a manner or a concession. 5. Notice what comes first and last, and what is split apart. 6. Read the sentence again in Latin order, without translating, to feel the build-up.

misunderstandings: A Latin participle does not have a fixed English translation. *affigentes* is not always 'fixing'; it can be 'while fixing', 'by fixing', 'having fixed' or 'who fix', depending on the sentence.

A word next to another is not necessarily joined to it. In *luce securitatis infusa* the participle *infusa* goes with *luce*, not with the genitive *securitatis* that stands between them; agreement decides.
Verb-last is not a rule, only a strong tendency in the formal prose of Cicero's school, which Augustine and Cyprian both inherit. They often put the verb earlier, and then it carries stress there.
Emphasis is a matter of interpretation. Say 'the order puts weight on …' where the order is plain, and do not claim to know what the author felt.

deeper.heading: Why the period lasted
body: The long periodic sentence was taught in the rhetorical schools in which Augustine taught and Cyprian was trained. Its aim was to build a sentence whose sense is complete only at its end. The Confessions is addressed to God as a prayer, yet its sentences often show this training: participles and subordinate matter first, and the main verb at the end.

examples.analysis: *trahentes* and *affigentes* are present participles in the nominative plural. *abierunt* and *manserunt* are the finite verbs. The sentence is built in two matching halves: those who went off to the palace were 'dragging their heart on the earth', and those who stayed in the hut were 'fixing their heart on heaven'. The two halves mirror each other, and the words *terra* and *caelo* stand in the same place in each, so that the contrast is plain.

examples.analysis: The perfect participle *infusa* agrees with the ablative *luce*, and the genitive *securitatis* stands between them: 'a light of security having been poured'. The dative *cordi meo* comes next. The subject *omnes … tenebrae* is split by the genitive *dubitationis*. The main verb, *diffugerunt*, 'fled in every direction', comes last, so that the whole image is built before the shadows disperse.

examples.analysis: *aperiebatur* is the main verb, but its subject, *casta dignitas continentiae*, appears only after two relative clauses that tell where she appeared. Then adjectives and participles in the nominative follow, all describing her, and the participle *extendens* governs *manus plenas gregibus bonorum exemplorum*, 'hands full of crowds of good examples'. The delay of the subject keeps the picture of Continence waiting.

examples.analysis: *potest* is the finite verb, the infinitive *peruenire* completes it, and *discordia* is its subject. The order puts the destination, *ad regnum caelorum*, first and the subject last. A reader who finds the verb and its subject sees at once what the sentence says: discord cannot reach the kingdom. The position of *discordia* makes it the closing word.

examples.analysis: *suspirabam* is the finite verb. *ligatus* is a perfect passive participle in the nominative singular masculine, agreeing with *ego*: 'I was sighing, bound'. The two phrases that follow set the bonds against each other: *non ferro alieno* is the iron of another, *sed mea ferrea uoluntate* is his own iron will. The repetition *ferro … ferrea* ties the two phrases to each other.

options: It is the main verb of the sentence.
It is an ablative absolute with *caelo*.
It is a gerund meaning 'by fixing'.
It is a participle in the nominative plural agreeing with *illi*: they stayed, fixing their heart on heaven.
practice.explain: *manserunt* is the finite verb. *affigentes* is a present active participle in the nominative plural, the same case and number as *illi*, and it says how the men stayed. It cannot be an ablative absolute because it does not agree with *caelo*, and a gerund has no case ending like this.

options: It sets the earthly heart against the heavenly one, and the two groups against each other.
It shows the two halves are one event, with no contrast.
It shows that the first half is a subordinate clause.
It makes the main verb of the first half belong to the second half.
practice.explain: Each half has a nominative participle, *cor*, a place, a finite verb and a second place. Because they match, the changed words (*in terra* and *caelo*, *abierunt* and *manserunt*) stand out as the contrast. Both halves are main clauses.

options: *luce*, in the ablative singular feminine; a genitive stands between them.
*meo*, because they are the last two words.
practice.explain: *infusa* is feminine singular and can be ablative; *luce* is feminine singular ablative. *securitatis* is genitive and *cordi meo* are dative, so neither can be joined to the participle. Nearness does not decide: agreement does.

options: The sentence is made a question.
The verb is made grammatically stronger.
The whole picture, the light poured in and the shadows of doubt, is built first, and the scattering comes as the last word.
The word *tenebrae* is changed to the genitive.
practice.explain: Latin word order does not change the case or the sense; it shifts the weight. A final verb after a long build-up gives the closing word the stress. The case of *tenebrae* is nominative plural in any position.

options: *rei*, the thing for which he sighed.
check.explain: *ligatus* is nominative singular masculine, and the nominative subject is *ego*. *rei* is dative feminine, *ferro* and *uoluntate* are ablative, and none of these could take the nominative masculine participle.

options: It makes the second phrase a subordinate clause.
It shows that both phrases name the same thing.
It sets an outward bond, another's iron, against an inward one, his own will, hard as iron.
check.explain: The *non … sed* contrast is plain, and the repeated *ferr-* links the two phrases: the bondage is called iron in both, but the second is his own. The two phrases are not identical in sense; they are opposed.

check.prompt: *sed illud placebat et uincebat, hoc libebat et uinciebat.* How are the two halves built?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: The first half is a main clause, the second a subordinate clause.
Both halves have the same subject, but they have different tenses.
The pronouns *illud* and *hoc* refer to the same thing.
The two halves are built alike, each with a pronoun and two verbs, and they set the better choice against the worse.
check.explain: Each half has a pronoun and a pair of imperfect verbs. *illud* (the former, giving himself to God's love) pleased and won; *hoc* (the latter, yielding to his own desire) was agreeable and bound him. *uincebat* and *uinciebat* sound alike on purpose. The two pronouns point at different things.

options: A gerund in the ablative: 'by reading'.
A present participle in the nominative, agreeing with the subject.
check.explain: *legendo* ends in *-ndo*, the ablative of the gerund, a verbal noun that tells the means. A present participle would be *legens*, and there is no noun with which *legendo* could agree.

options: A dative of the person who closed the book.
An ablative absolute: a finger or some other mark having been put in, I closed the book.
A genitive absolute telling whose book it was.
check.explain: A participle and its nouns stand in the ablative, apart from the rest of the sentence's grammar: that is the ablative absolute. It tells the circumstance in which the book was closed. Classical Latin has no genitive absolute, though Greek does.

options: Two datives telling to whom Victorinus was a child.
Two ablative absolutes in matching form, naming the bowed neck and the tamed forehead as the manner of his submission.
check.explain: Each ablative absolute has a perfect participle and a noun (*subiecto collo*, *edomita fronte*), and each is followed by a phrase with *ad*. The two are parallel in form, and the pair describes how Victorinus submitted. The subject of *erubuerit* is Victorinus, understood from the earlier part of the sentence.

check.prompt: *ad regnum caelorum non potest peruenire discordia.* Which word is the subject, and what does its position do?

quoted.title: On the Unity of the Church (De ecclesiae catholicae unitate)
quoted.reference: Cyprian of Carthage, On the Unity of the Church (De ecclesiae catholicae unitate) 14
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: *caelorum*; it is the genitive of the possessor.
*regnum*; it stands first so that it is stressed.
*potest*; it is the verb and so comes in the middle.
*discordia*; it stands last, and so it closes the sentence with stress.
check.explain: *discordia* is nominative singular, the only form that can be the subject. *regnum* is the accusative object of the preposition *ad*, and *caelorum* is genitive. In this sentence the destination comes first and the subject last, so the last word bears the weight.

check.prompt: *mansit ergo ille ubi sedebamus nimie stupens.* What does *stupens* describe?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A different person who is not named.
check.explain: *stupens* is a nominative singular participle, and *ille* is the nominative singular subject of *mansit*. It says how he stayed: struck with wonder. *sedebamus* is a finite verb in a clause of place, and Augustine is the one who has gone away.

check.prompt: *aperiebatur enim ab ea parte … casta dignitas continentiae …* Which is the subject of *aperiebatur*, and why is it not at the start?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: *dignitas*, which is held back until the clauses telling where she appeared have been said.
*parte*; the clause of place comes first.
check.explain: *aperiebatur* is third person singular, so it needs a nominative singular subject; *casta dignitas* is that subject, and *continentiae* is a genitive depending on it. The writer set it after the two relative clauses, so that the reader must wait to see who appeared.

reading.reference: Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 8.28 – Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 8.30
reading.why: The last three sections of the garden scene: the storm of tears, the voice and the opened book, and the aftermath. They contain a long periodic sentence with a final verb (8.29), an ablative absolute (8.30), and participles in the nominative that tell how things were done.
